title: preemptible-shard-admission-with-reserve-windows-and-degradation-pipeline
creator: Marcus Li
description:
Problem: During bursty multi-region traffic and partial regional failovers we observe tail-latency SLO erosion for low-priority tenants and increased cascading retries from client SDKs. Existing admission gates are binary (accept/reject) and current degradation modes are coarse-grained (model swap or outright reject).

Goal: Implement a hybrid load-shedding mechanism that combines short-lived token reservations (reserve windows) with preemptible shard lanes and an orchestrated degradation pipeline. The mechanism should: 1) protect P0/P1 tenants and critical control-plane requests, 2) provide graceful, observable fidelity degradation for best-effort tenants, and 3) integrate with autoscaler and circuit-breaker signals for multi-region failover scenarios.

Design summary:
- Reservation windows: allocate small, expirations-based token reservations for latency-sensitive requests at the front door. A reservation is a timebox (e.g., 150ms) that guarantees admission to a low-latency lane if capacity is available. Unused reservations expire and are returned to the pool.
- Preemptible shard lanes: tag a subset of worker shards as preemptible. These shards accept only lower-priority workload and can be reclaimed instantly under pressure. Preemptible lanes run cheaper instance types or heavier quantized execution to reduce unit cost.
- Admission controller handshake: when a request arrives, the admission controller checks (a) reservation tokens, (b) tenant priority, (c) real-time shard capacity, and (d) circuit-breaker state. If capacity exists on non-preemptible lanes, route there. Otherwise route to preemptible lane with a required degraded-policy.
- Degradation pipeline: for requests routed to preemptible lanes apply ordered degradation steps with idempotent transformations and quality heuristics: partial-output (early-stopping), compressible-context-trimming (prefix drop), structured-field-dropping (non-essential fields), fallback-to-smaller-model-variant, and finally queueing-with-timeout. Each step is observable and reversible.
- Rollback windows & escalation: preemptible decisions carry a rollback TTL. If downstream metrics (tail latency, error rate, measured quality) cross thresholds, the system either increase reservations, shift capacity, or trigger multi-region failover through the circuit breaker.

Why different from existing controllers: this combines short-lived soft reservations with preemptible capacity and staged degradations rather than single-step trimming or all-or-nothing shedding. It aims for predictable tail protection and operational clarity for SRE and customer-support teams.

updates: 2026-02-28 - Kickoff: scoped design with SRE, Runtime, and Console. Decided on 150ms default reservation window. Action: runtime spike and dashboard prototype.

2026-03-03 - Spike complete: implemented reservation proto in staging admission-gateway. Observed reservations reduced rejected requests by 22% in synthetic tail-bursts. Draft PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4273

2026-03-06 - Design review with ML infra and Product. Trade-off: preemptible shards increase scheduling complexity but reduce cost by allowing lower-spec instances. PM asked to include quota impacts for Dedicated customers.

2026-03-09 - Load test (staging, multi-region sim): 3x burst with two-region failover scenario. Results: P0 99th latency within SLO, P3 tenants experienced higher quality degradation but fewer outright rejections. Perf notes saved to Confluence: https://confluence.redwood.ai/pages/AdaptiveSheddingSpike

2026-03-12 - Implementation: added telemetry hooks and degradation-step counters. Added unit + integration tests for reservation expiry and preemption handshake. Feature gated under runtime.feature.preemptible_admission.

2026-03-14 - Ops review: created initial operator playbook draft (Console runbook doc). Raised follow-up tasks: tuning heuristics for emb-heavy requests and a canary plan for Dedicated clusters. Assigned to Aisha for rollout plan.
tradeoffs_and_notes: Reservations reduce immediate rejections but can introduce a small head-of-line hold if mis-sized; we default to short windows (100-200ms) to limit impact.
Preemptible shards simplify reclamation but complicate autoscaler heuristics; will iterate on autoscaler handshake to notify shard role changes before eviction.
Degradation sequencing prioritizes reversible and low-cost steps first (trimming and early-stop) before model swaps to maintain perceived quality.
Will need careful Dedicated customer negotiation: preemptible lanes should never host tenant-pinned reserved capacity unless explicitly configured.
Metrics budget: adding reservation and rollback metrics will increase cardinality—keep labels coarse (priority-band, region, degraded-step) to control prometheus cardinality.
Security: no PII is removed during trimming; ensure audit logs record when structured fields are dropped for compliance investigations.
